blocks.content: You have designed your classes, mapped your objects, drawn your sequences. Everything looks good at the code level.
But then someone asks: "How does the entire system actually fit together? Which parts talk to which? What depends on what?"
That is the question a Component Diagram answers.

Where a class diagram zooms into the internal structure of code, a component diagram zooms out to show the bigger building blocks the modules, services, and libraries that make up the whole system and how they wire together.
1. What is a Component Diagram?
A Component Diagram is a structural UML diagram that shows how a system is divided into components and how those components connect and depend on each other.
A component is any replaceable, self-contained piece of the system that has a clear interface a service, a module, a library, a database, an external API.
Three things it tells you:
["What the major building blocks of the system are","What each component exposes and what it needs from others","How data and control flow between components"]
items: What the major building blocks of the system are
What each component exposes and what it needs from others
How data and control flow between components

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802627-0901503e.png
This is not about classes or objects. It is about the chunks the system is carved into and the contracts between them.
2. Components of a Component Diagram
Every component diagram is assembled from four building blocks.
1. Component

A component is a self-contained unit of the system with a well-defined boundary. It can be deployed, replaced, or tested independently. Drawn as a rectangle with the <> stereotype or a small component icon in the corner.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802720-9aaea229.png

Good components have one clear responsibility. AuthService handles authentication and nothing else. NotificationService sends alerts and nothing else. If a component needs two labels to describe what it does, it probably needs to be split.
2. Interface
An interface defines the contract a component exposes to the outside world. There are two sides to every interface:

["Provided interface what the component offers to others. Drawn as a lollipop (circle on a stick).","Required interface what the component needs from others to do its job. Drawn as a socket (half circle)."]
items: Provided interface what the component offers to others. Drawn as a lollipop (circle on a stick).
Required interface what the component needs from others to do its job. Drawn as a socket (half circle).

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802811-d86477d5.png
Account Service requires the IAuthService interface. Auth Service provides it. The two components never need to know each other's internals they only need to agree on the interface between them.
3. Dependencies
A dependency shows that one component relies on another. Drawn as a dashed arrow pointing from the dependent component to the one it depends on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802955-28811ce9.png
Transaction Service cannot do its job without Account Service and Fraud Detection Service. If either one changes its interface, Transaction Service needs to know about it.
4. Subsystems and Boundaries
Related components can be grouped inside a boundary box to show they belong together a subsystem, a layer, or a deployment unit.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245803266-4a6d8d22.png
Boundaries make large diagrams readable. Instead of seeing twenty components floating freely, you see three groups with clear responsibilities.
Component Diagram vs Other Diagrams
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245803748-4b3cef78.jpg

A class diagram tells you what TransactionService looks like inside. A sequence diagram shows how it behaves during a transfer. A component diagram shows where it sits in the overall system and what it connects to.
When to Use a Component Diagram
blocks.text: When to Use a Component Diagram

blocks.content: Reach for a component diagram when:

["Planning a new system map out the major pieces before writing a single class","Onboarding new team members one diagram communicates the architecture faster than hours of explanation","Designing microservices show which services exist, what they own, and how they talk to each other","Identifying coupling a component with ten dependency arrows pointing out of it is a warning sign","Planning a refactor visualize what currently depends on what before moving anything"]
items: Planning a new system map out the major pieces before writing a single class
Onboarding new team members one diagram communicates the architecture faster than hours of explanation
Designing microservices show which services exist, what they own, and how they talk to each other
Identifying coupling a component with ten dependency arrows pointing out of it is a warning sign
Planning a refactor visualize what currently depends on what before moving anything

blocks.content: 3. Complete Example: Banking System Architecture

The scenario: A digital banking platform. Customers access it through a mobile app and a web app. Behind the scenes multiple services handle authentication, accounts, transactions, notifications, and fraud detection. Each service owns its own database.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245804037-4deec33e.png
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: Reading the diagram

Client Layer Both the mobile app and web app sit here. They never talk directly to any service everything goes through the API Gateway. This single entry point handles rate limiting and routing so the individual services never have to worry about it.

Gateway Layer The API Gateway is the front door of the entire backend. Every request lands here first. It figures out which service should handle it and forwards it along. Centralising this logic here means adding a new service does not require every client to update how it communicates.

Core Services Five independent services each owning one responsibility. Auth Service handles login and token validation. Account Service manages account data. Transaction Service processes transfers and payments. Fraud Detection Service analyses patterns and flags suspicious activity. Notification Service dispatches emails and SMS alerts.

Notice the dependencies inside this layer. When Transaction Service processes a transfer it reaches out to Account Service to verify the account exists, to Fraud Detection Service to clear the transaction, and to Notification Service to alert the customer. It also calls the Central Bank API for interbank transfers. Every one of these is an explicit dependency, visible on the diagram and impossible to miss.

Data Layer Each service owns its own database. This is a deliberate design choice. Transaction Service cannot directly query Account DB it must go through Account Service. This keeps the services truly independent and makes each one replaceable without cascading changes.

External Layer Three things live outside the system boundary. The email provider, the SMS gateway, and the Central Bank API are all third-party dependencies. Only Notification Service talks to the email and SMS providers. Only Transaction Service talks to the Central Bank. Containing these external dependencies inside specific services means swapping providers only ever affects one component.
4. Component Granularity and Where the Diagram Fits
blocks.text: 4. Component Granularity and Where the Diagram Fits

blocks.content: A component is not the same size as a class. A single component like AuthModule can wrap half a dozen classes, LoginController, TokenValidator, PasswordHasher, SessionStore, behind one exposed interface. The component diagram does not care what is inside that box. It only cares what the box promises to the rest of the system.
Class Grain vs Component Grain

A class diagram shows the fields and methods of LoginController itself, down to individual method signatures. A component diagram hides all of that and shows only the module boundary, AuthModule, and the interface it exposes, IAuthCheck. Anyone reading the component diagram does not need to know that AuthModule internally uses three helper classes to do its job, they only need to know it accepts a credential and returns a validated identity.

["AuthModule bundles LoginController, TokenValidator, and PasswordHasher behind a single IAuthCheck interface","PaymentModule bundles PaymentGateway, RefundHandler, and InvoiceBuilder behind a single IPaymentProcessor interface","InventoryModule bundles StockTracker, WarehouseSync, and ReorderPlanner behind a single IStockReserve interface"]
items: AuthModule bundles LoginController, TokenValidator, and PasswordHasher behind a single IAuthCheck interface
PaymentModule bundles PaymentGateway, RefundHandler, and InvoiceBuilder behind a single IPaymentProcessor interface
InventoryModule bundles StockTracker, WarehouseSync, and ReorderPlanner behind a single IStockReserve interface

blocks.content: The Assembly Connector: Provided Meets Required
blocks.text: The Assembly Connector: Provided Meets Required

blocks.content: Earlier sections drew the provided lollipop and the required socket as two separate symbols hanging off two separate components. In a real diagram the two are usually drawn wired directly together, the socket of one component plugged straight into the lollipop of the other. This combined shape is called an assembly connector, and it is the most common way component diagrams show a live connection rather than just a listed capability.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783498450022-848964387.png
blocks.alt: Account Module requiring the IAuthCheck interface that Auth Module provides, wired together as an assembly connector

blocks.content: AccountModule requires IAuthCheck. AuthModule provides IAuthCheck. The assembly connector between them is the diagram's way of saying these two components are wired together right now, not just theoretically compatible.
Where a Component Diagram Sits Between Architecture and Class Views
blocks.text: Where a Component Diagram Sits Between Architecture and Class Views

blocks.content: Think of system design as a set of zoom levels. At the widest zoom, a system architecture diagram shows entire systems, a mobile app, a backend, a database, a third party payment provider, as single boxes. At the narrowest zoom, a class diagram shows the fields and methods inside one class. A component diagram sits in the middle. It zooms in past whole applications and external systems, but it stops well before showing a single method signature.

{"headers":["Zoom level","Typical unit shown","Answers"],"rows":[["System architecture diagram","Whole applications and external systems","Which systems exist and how do they talk over the network"],["Component diagram","Modules, services, and libraries inside one system","What are the pieces inside this system and what does each expose"],["Class diagram","Individual classes, fields, and methods","How is one piece actually built"],["Sequence diagram","Method calls over time between objects","In what order do things happen during one use case"]]}

A team planning a new backend usually moves through these zoom levels in order. Draw the architecture diagram first to agree on the systems involved. Draw the component diagram next to agree on the modules inside the backend and their interfaces. Only then do individual engineers draw class diagrams for the module they own.
5. Worked Example: E-Commerce Checkout

Consider a checkout flow for an online store. A shopper has items in a cart and clicks pay. Behind that one click, several components need to cooperate, confirm the cart contents, reserve stock, charge a card, and create an order record.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783498451681-575107457.png
blocks.alt: Cart, Payment, and Inventory components connected to a central Order component through ICartSummary, IPaymentProcessor, and IStockReserve interfaces

blocks.content: Reading the Diagram

Cart Component holds the shopper's selected items and their quantities. It exposes ICartSummary so any other part of the system can ask what is currently in a given cart without knowing how the cart is stored.

Order Component is the coordinator. When the shopper confirms checkout, Order Component requires ICartSummary from Cart Component to know what is being bought, requires IPaymentProcessor from Payment Component to charge the card, and requires IStockReserve from Inventory Component to hold the items before confirming the order.

Payment Component provides IPaymentProcessor. Internally it might call a third party payment gateway, retry failed charges, or generate receipts, none of which appears on this diagram. Order Component only sees the one interface it needs.
Inventory Component provides IStockReserve. It decides how stock is tracked across warehouses and what happens when an item is nearly out of stock, details that stay entirely inside its own boundary.

{"headers":["Component","Provides","Requires"],"rows":[["Cart Component","ICartSummary","None"],["Payment Component","IPaymentProcessor","None"],["Inventory Component","IStockReserve","None"],["Order Component","IOrderStatus","ICartSummary, IPaymentProcessor, IStockReserve"]]}
Why Split It This Way

Splitting checkout into four components instead of one large CheckoutService pays off the first time something changes. Swap the payment gateway from one provider to another and only Payment Component changes, its IPaymentProcessor interface stays the same so Order Component never notices. Add a second warehouse and only Inventory Component changes. A single monolithic CheckoutService would force every one of those changes to touch the same file, tested by the same suite, deployed as one unit.

["Each component can be tested in isolation by mocking the interfaces it requires","Each component can be owned by a different team without stepping on each other's code","Each component can be replaced or scaled independently as long as its interface stays stable"]
items: Each component can be tested in isolation by mocking the interfaces it requires
Each component can be owned by a different team without stepping on each other's code
Each component can be replaced or scaled independently as long as its interface stays stable
